cea_yield_lettuce.unit: kg fresh per m2 per year
cea_yield_lettuce.what: Lettuce yield in an indoor vertical farm with artificial light (review table 'Summary of annual data for an indoor vertical farm', citing Coyle and Ellison 2017); per m2 of land with stacked layers implied. Same review gives 41 kg/m2/year for greenhouse and 3.9 kg/m2/year for open field. Avgoustaki & Xydis 2020, doi 10.1016/bs.af2s.2020.08.002.

more.unit: g edible dry mass per m2 per day
more.what: Lettuce cv. Waldmann's Green, 4 crops in NASA Biomass Production Chamber, 16 h photoperiod at 280-336 umol m-2 s-1 (16.1-19.4 mol m-2 d-1), 28-30 day crops. Wheeler et al. 2003, NASA/TM-2003-211184, Table 7 'Yields and PAR levels for ALS crops' (NASA Kennedy Space Center Biomass Production Chamber, 20 m2 closed chamber, HPS lamps, hydroponic NFT, ~1000-1200 ppm CO2). Table is a rotated scan; rows read from the page image (PDF page 29). Columns: Photoper./PPF (h / umol m-2 s-1); Daily PAR (mol m-2 d-1); Total biomass kg m-2, g m-2 d-1, g/mol PAR; Edible biomass kg m-2, g m-2 d-1, g/mol PAR.

more.unit: g dry biomass per m2 per day (380 g fresh per m2 per day)
more.what: Highest lettuce productivity at PPF 1000 umol m-2 s-1 (57.6 mol m-2 d-1), CO2 1200 ppm, ~30 C, tipburn prevented by airflow; averaged over 23 days of light. Frantz et al. 2004, J. Amer. Soc. Hort. Sci. 129:331 (abstract). Note the abstract prints the fresh figure as '380 g d-1 fresh mass' (per m2 implied).
more.quote: The highest productivity was 19 g m-2 d-1 of dry biomass (380 g d-1 fresh mass) averaged over the 23 days the plants received light.

more.unit: kg fresh per m2 per year
more.what: Median lettuce productivity of research vertical-farm settings (per m2 of cultivation surface), as reviewed by Pennisi et al. 2025 and cited in Jadhav et al. 2026 (Front. Plant Sci., doi 10.3389/fpls.2026.1827422); the same study measured 20-32 kg FW m-2 year-1 for baby-leaf lettuce at 200 umol m-2 s-1.
more.quote: Our findings fall within the wide range of lettuce productivity of research settings reviewed by Pennisi et al. (2025), centered on a median of 48.3 kg m-2 year-1.

more.unit: g fresh per m2 per day
more.what: Romaine lettuce in greenhouses vs 10 g/m2/day in traditional farming (Avgoustaki & Xydis 2020 citing Pennisi et al. 2019).
more.quote: According to Penissi et al. (2019) greenhouses produce 112 g of fresh weight of romaine lettuce per m2 daily while traditional farming produce 10 g of fresh weight of romaine lettuce per m2 per day.

cea_yield_tomato.unit: kg fresh per m2 (average greenhouse yield, annual crop)
cea_yield_tomato.what: Average fresh tomato yield of high-tech Dutch greenhouses (vs 7-9 kg m-2 in Italian greenhouses), as stated in Palmitessa et al. 2021, Antioxidants 10:687. The sentence does not print 'per year'; it is the average yield of the (year-round) crop.
cea_yield_tomato.quote: At the same time, tomato is the most cultivated species in Netherlands greenhouses with almost 15,000 ha with an average yield of 60–70 kg m−2 [2].

more.unit: g edible dry mass per m2 per day
more.what: Tomato (2 crops) in NASA Biomass Production Chamber, 12 h photoperiod at 615 and 894 umol m-2 s-1 (26.6 and 38.6 mol m-2 d-1). Wheeler et al. 2003, NASA/TM-2003-211184, Table 7 'Yields and PAR levels for ALS crops' (NASA Kennedy Space Center Biomass Production Chamber, 20 m2 closed chamber, HPS lamps, hydroponic NFT, ~1000-1200 ppm CO2). Table is a rotated scan; rows read from the page image (PDF page 29). Columns: Photoper./PPF (h / umol m-2 s-1); Daily PAR (mol m-2 d-1); Total biomass kg m-2, g m-2 d-1, g/mol PAR; Edible biomass kg m-2, g m-2 d-1, g/mol PAR.

cea_yield_potato.unit: g edible (tuber) dry mass per m2 per day
cea_yield_potato.what: Potato, 5 crops in NASA Biomass Production Chamber, 12 h (one 12-16 h) photoperiod at 655-917 umol m-2 s-1 (28.3-42.7 mol m-2 d-1). Wheeler et al. 2003, NASA/TM-2003-211184, Table 7 'Yields and PAR levels for ALS crops' (NASA Kennedy Space Center Biomass Production Chamber, 20 m2 closed chamber, HPS lamps, hydroponic NFT, ~1000-1200 ppm CO2). Table is a rotated scan; rows read from the page image (PDF page 29). Columns: Photoper./PPF (h / umol m-2 s-1); Daily PAR (mol m-2 d-1); Total biomass kg m-2, g m-2 d-1, g/mol PAR; Edible biomass kg m-2, g m-2 d-1, g/mol PAR.

more.unit: g tuber dry mass per m2 per day
more.what: Potato in University of Wisconsin growth rooms: 21.9 for a solid stand grown 15 weeks under continuous light at 400 umol m-2 s-1, 16 C, 1000 ppm CO2; 32.8 for separated plants with side lighting. Tibbitts & Wheeler 1987, Adv. Space Res. 7(4):115 (abstract).
more.quote: A productivity of 21.9 g m-2 day-1 of edible tubers from a solid stand of potatoes grown for 15 weeks with continuous irradiation at 400 micromoles s-1 m-2, 16 degrees C and 1000 microliters l-1 CO2 has been obtained.

more.unit: g tuber dry mass per m2 per day
more.what: Potato cv. Norland, 24 h photoperiod, 16 C, maximum tuber productivity at 126 days (19.5 under 12 h photoperiod); 148-day yield equates to ~40 t/ha dry (200 t fresh). Wheeler & Tibbitts 1987, Am. Potato J. 64:311 (abstract).
more.quote: Tuber productivity (g m-2 day-1) under the 24-h photoperiod reached a maximum of 29.4 g dwt m-2 day-1 at 126 days, but continued to rise throughout the experiment under the 12-h photoperiod, reaching 19.5 g dwt m-2 day-1

cea_yield_wheat.unit: g edible (grain) dry mass per m2 per day
cea_yield_wheat.what: Wheat cv. Yecora Rojo, 5 crops in NASA Biomass Production Chamber, 20-24 h photoperiod at 535-1177 umol m-2 s-1 (38.5-84.7 mol m-2 d-1). Wheeler et al. 2003, NASA/TM-2003-211184, Table 7 'Yields and PAR levels for ALS crops' (NASA Kennedy Space Center Biomass Production Chamber, 20 m2 closed chamber, HPS lamps, hydroponic NFT, ~1000-1200 ppm CO2). Table is a rotated scan; rows read from the page image (PDF page 29). Columns: Photoper./PPF (h / umol m-2 s-1); Daily PAR (mol m-2 d-1); Total biomass kg m-2, g m-2 d-1, g/mol PAR; Edible biomass kg m-2, g m-2 d-1, g/mol PAR.

more.unit: g grain (dry) per m2 per day
more.what: Record wheat grain yield in a near-optimum controlled environment at the highest PPF (up to 2080 umol m-2 s-1, 150 mol m-2 d-1, 16-20 h photoperiod), CO2 1200 ppm, hydroponic, 2000 plants/m2; crop growth rate 138 g m-2 d-1. Bugbee & Salisbury 1988, Plant Physiol. 88:869 (abstract).
more.quote: Crop growth rate and grain yield reached 138 and 60 grams per square meter per day, respectively; both continued to increase up to the highest integrated daily PPF level, which was three times greater than a typical daily flux in the field.

more.unit: t grain per hectare of growing layer per year (= 7.0 to 19.4 kg per m2 per year, at 11% grain moisture)
more.what: Indoor wheat per single layer: 700 t/ha/yr measured-and-scaled for 10 layers (Monje & Bugbee experiment: 20 h of 1400 umol m-2 s-1, 330 ppm CO2, 70-day crop, 5 harvests/yr) up to 1940 t/ha/yr simulated for 10 layers (1800-2000 umol m-2 s-1 for 24 h, 1200 ppm CO2, harvest index 0.64); the paper states '194 t/ha/y x 10 layers'; the 70 t/ha/layer figure is 700/10. Asseng et al. 2020, PNAS 117:19131.
more.quote: A 1-ha, 10-layer indoor wheat facility developed as a vertical farm (27) or plant factory (28) (SI Appendix) could produce up to 1,940 ± 230 t/ha/y (194 t/ha/y × 10 layers), approximately 600 times the current average global yield in the field (Fig. 2).

cea_yield_soybean.unit: g edible (seed) dry mass per m2 per day
cea_yield_soybean.what: Soybean cv. McCall, 4 crops in NASA Biomass Production Chamber, 10-12 h photoperiod at 477-855 umol m-2 s-1 (20.6-36.9 mol m-2 d-1), 90-97 day crops. Wheeler et al. 2003, NASA/TM-2003-211184, Table 7 'Yields and PAR levels for ALS crops' (NASA Kennedy Space Center Biomass Production Chamber, 20 m2 closed chamber, HPS lamps, hydroponic NFT, ~1000-1200 ppm CO2). Table is a rotated scan; rows read from the page image (PDF page 29). Columns: Photoper./PPF (h / umol m-2 s-1); Daily PAR (mol m-2 d-1); Total biomass kg m-2, g m-2 d-1, g/mol PAR; Edible biomass kg m-2, g m-2 d-1, g/mol PAR.

more.unit: m2 of vertical-farm crop area per adult for the yearly protein requirement (soy as only protein source)
more.what: Soybean in a vertical farm: protein yield per m2 about eight times open field; yearly protein of one reference adult needs 20 m2 crop area, 2.4 m3 water and 16 MWh electricity (vs 164 m2 in the field). Righini et al. 2024, J. Sci. Food Agric., doi 10.1002/jsfa.13458 (abstract).
more.quote: Assuming soy as the only protein source in the diet, the resources needed to get total yearly protein requirement of a reference adult would be 20 m2 of crop area, 2.4 m3 of water and 16 MWh of electricity, versus 164 m2, 111 m3 and 0.009 MWh in the field.

cea_yield_pepper.unit: kg marketable fresh fruit per m2 (accumulated marketable yield over one crop's harvest period, winter to summer; not a per-year figure)
cea_yield_pepper.what: Sweet pepper in a heated greenhouse in Iceland under high-pressure sodium lamps: ~25 kg m-2 at 160 W m-2 top lighting; ~36 kg m-2 at 160 W m-2 top + 120 W m-2 interlighting with 4.5 plants m-2. Stadler 2026, PeerJ, doi 10.7717/peerj.21491.
cea_yield_pepper.quote: At the lowest light intensity (TL 160), the accumulated marketable yield was not significantly affected by plant density (approximately 25 kg m−2 for both 3.0 and 4.5 plants m−2) (Fig. 3). In contrast, at the highest light intensity (TL 160 + IL 120), marketable yield was significantly higher at the higher plant density of 4.5 plants m−2 compared to 3.0 plants m−2, with yields of approximately 36 kg m−2 and 30 kg m−2, respectively.

cea_area_per_person.unit: m2 of crop growing area per person
cea_area_per_person.what: NASA (Wheeler 2014, 'NASA's Controlled Environment Agriculture Testing for Space Habitats', NTRS 20140017323), from Bios-3 and NASA Biomass Production Chamber testing under electric light with hydroponics and CO2 enrichment: about 20-25 m2 supplies one person's O2; about 50 m2 supplies dietary calories (2500 kcal/person/day, staple-crop vegetarian diet); a more complete diet needs more area.
cea_area_per_person.quote: Based on the findings from the Russian Bios-3 project and NASA testing, about 20-25 m2 of crops could supply the O2 for one human, while about 50 m2 would be required for dietary calories (2500 kcal person-1 d-1). To provide all the spices, and flavors for a more complete diet would require more planted area (Masuda et al., 2005; Tako et al., 2010).

more.unit: m2 per person
more.what: Area of potatoes alone to supply 2800 kcal/day: 34.3 m2 at 21.9 g m-2 d-1 (continuous light, 400 umol m-2 s-1), 23.6 m2 at 32.8 g m-2 d-1 with side lighting. Tibbitts & Wheeler 1987 (abstract).
more.quote: This equates to an area of 34.3 m2 being required to provide 2800 kcal of potatoes per day for a human diet. Separated plants receiving side lighting have produced 32.8 g m-2 day-1 which equates to an area of 23.6 m2 to provide 2800 kcal.

more.unit: m2 per person
more.what: Optimistic CELSS estimates quoted in Ellery 2021 (Life 11:770): 10 m2/person with elevated temperature, hydroponics and high CO2 gives full O2 but only 50% of food (20 m2 assumed for food). Same paper: 6.6 m2/person for wheat vs 20.1 m2/person for rice, and a 528 m2 greenhouse for 18 astronauts (21 crops, 100% of nutrition).
more.quote: An agricultural footprint of 10 m2 is sufficient to provide full O2 generation and 200% water requirement per person through photosynthesis but only 50% food requirement (assuming 20 m2 required for food production).

cea_light_ppfd.what: PPF used for each crop in NASA Biomass Production Chamber tests (HPS lamps; photoperiods 16 h lettuce, 20-24 h wheat, 10-12 h soybean, 12 h potato and tomato). Wheeler et al. 2003, NASA/TM-2003-211184, Table 7 'Yields and PAR levels for ALS crops' (NASA Kennedy Space Center Biomass Production Chamber, 20 m2 closed chamber, HPS lamps, hydroponic NFT, ~1000-1200 ppm CO2). Table is a rotated scan; rows read from the page image (PDF page 29). Columns: Photoper./PPF (h / umol m-2 s-1); Daily PAR (mol m-2 d-1); Total biomass kg m-2, g m-2 d-1, g/mol PAR; Edible biomass kg m-2, g m-2 d-1, g/mol PAR.

more.unit: umol m-2 s-1
more.what: Typical light intensity for crops suited to commercial plant factories with artificial lighting (leafy crops, 30-60 day cultivation). Kozai 2013, Proc. Jpn. Acad. Ser. B 89:447.
more.quote: Accordingly, plants suitable for production in CPPS are those that can be grown at high planting density (50–1,000 plants/m2) to the harvestable stage under relatively low light intensity (100–300 µmol m−2 s−1) and within a short cultivation period (30–60 days).

more.unit: umol m-2 s-1
more.what: Wheat at maximum-yield lighting: Monje & Bugbee experiment 20 h/d at 1400; near-linear growth response up to 2000. Asseng et al. 2020, PNAS.
more.quote: In the indoor experiment reported by Monje and Bugbee (13), the wheat was grown under 20 h per day of light at an intensity of 1,400 μmol/m2/s, totaling 50 MJ/m2/d (with 1 J = 1 Ws), and an atmospheric CO2 concentration of 330 ppm. However, wheat can utilize light for photosynthesis and growth for up to 24 h per day (17, 18) with an almost linear crop growth response up to 2,000 μmol/m2/s (19, 20).

more.unit: umol m-2 s-1
more.what: Lettuce high-light limit study: PPF raised to 1000 (57.6 mol m-2 d-1), 'two to three times higher than normally used for lettuce'. Frantz et al. 2004 (abstract).
more.quote: We eliminated tipburn by blowing air directly onto the meristem, which allowed us to increase the photosynthetic photon flux (PPF) to 1000 micromoles m-2 s-1 (57.6 mol m-2 d-1); two to three times higher than normally used for lettuce.

led_efficacy.unit: umol per joule (fixture photon efficacy, 400-700 nm)
led_efficacy.what: Achieved efficacy of horticultural LED fixtures as of 2020: 2.5-2.8 for white+red, 3.0 for blue+red; typical 2-3; calculated currently possible 3.4 (white+red) and 4.1 (blue+red); best fixtures in 2014 were 1.7; DLC listing minimum 1.9. Physical maxima: 3.76 for 450 nm blue, 5.52 for 660 nm red photons. Kusuma, Pattison & Bugbee 2020, Horticulture Research 7:56.
led_efficacy.quote: Now, fixture efficacies of 2.5 to 2.8 µmol J−1 for white + red fixtures and 3 µmol J−1 for blue + red fixtures have been achieved (Table 2).

more.unit: umol per joule
more.what: Calculated currently-possible fixture efficacy vs typical 2-3. Kusuma et al. 2020.
more.quote: The calculations in this paper show current possible performance levels of LED fixtures of 3.4 µmol J−1 for white + red fixtures, and 4.1 µmol J−1 for blue + red fixtures. These values are significantly higher than current typical values of 2–3 µmol J−1.

more.unit: umol per joule
more.what: Efficacy of the commercial full-spectrum LED bars used in a 2026 lettuce vertical-farming trial (Palmitessa et al. 2026, Front. Plant Sci., doi 10.3389/fpls.2026.1783548).
more.quote: a photosynthetic photon flux (PPF) of 80–200 µmol s⁻¹ and efficiency ranging from 3.0 to 3.4 µmol J⁻¹.

cea_lighting_power.unit: kWh of lamp electricity per m2 of cultivation area per day (about 129 W/m2 averaged over the 16 h photoperiod; the W/m2 figure is my division, not printed in the source)
cea_lighting_power.what: LED lighting electricity in a vertical-farm lettuce (baby leaf) trial at total PPFD 200 umol m-2 s-1, 16 h photoperiod (06:00-22:00), constant red/blue control treatment; metered with power meters. Jadhav et al. 2026, Front. Plant Sci., Table 1.
cea_lighting_power.quote: Treatment | Red light (µmol m-2 s-1) | Blue light (µmol m-2 s-1) | ... | Total PPFD(µmol m-2 s-1) | Energy use (kWh m-2 d-1) | Control (constant) | 150 | 50 | – | – | Constant spectrum | 200 | 2.06

more.unit: W of input electrical power per m2 of growing area
more.what: NASA Biomass Production Chamber: 96 x 400 W high-pressure sodium lamps on dimming ballasts over 20 m2 (full power; delivered up to ~1177 umol m-2 s-1). Wheeler et al. 2003, NASA/TM-2003-211184.
more.quote: Lighting was provided by 96 400-W high-pressure sodium (HPS) lamps operated on dimming ballasts, thereby providing about 2 kW of input electrical power per m2of growing area.

more.unit: W per m2 (installed HPS supplemental lighting)
more.what: Greenhouse sweet pepper winter production in Iceland: top lighting 160 or 240 W m-2, or top 120-160 + interlighting 120 W m-2. Stadler 2026, PeerJ.

more.unit: kWh of LED electricity per m2 per 26-day growth cycle
more.what: Lettuce in a vertical-farm growth chamber at DLI 14.4 mol m-2 d-1 (PPFD 170 at the 24 h photoperiod; higher at shorter photoperiods), LEDs of 3.0-3.4 umol/J. Palmitessa et al. 2026.
more.quote: During the growth cycle, the average LEDs electrical consumption was 130 kWh·m-2, independently to light treatments (Table 4).

cea_energy_lettuce.unit: kWh of electricity per kg of fresh lettuce (whole farm: lighting, climate control, pumping)
cea_energy_lettuce.what: Vertical farms: a modelled Swedish commercial vertical farm uses 10 kWh/kg; the literature average is roughly 20 kWh/kg. 'Environmental implications of lettuce sourcing: Comparison of sourcing from vertical farms and conventional production' (2025, PMC11759643).
cea_energy_lettuce.quote: For instance, the modelled VFS requires 10 kWh per kilogram of lettuce produced while the average VFS in literature uses roughly 20 kWh/kg [33].

more.unit: kWh per kg fresh lettuce
more.what: Commercial vertical farm: ~5 million kWh for ~500,000 kg lettuce per year (Martin et al. 2023), as quoted in Lovat, Noor & Milo 2025, Plant Physiology (doi 10.1093/plphys/kiaf056); same paper: ~250 kWh per kg of dry plant matter at 2% energetic efficiency.
more.quote: For example, Martin et al. 2023 report ≈5 million kWh of electricity usage in a commercial vertical farm producing ≈500,000 kg of lettuce annually, equaling 10 kWh of electricity per kg of lettuce.

more.unit: kWh per kg lettuce
more.what: UK vertical-farm lettuce, 'hyperlocal' deployment scenario (Gargaro et al. 2026, doi 10.1016/j.clfs.2026.100037, Table 3).
more.quote: VF lettuce (hyperlocal scenario)|0.932|17.25|590

more.unit: kWh of electricity per kg of DRY matter
more.what: Plant factory with fluorescent lamps (Kozai 2013): 0.7% of electricity converted to chemical energy in dry matter; at ~5% dry matter this is ~40 kWh per kg fresh (my multiplication, not in source).
more.quote: Thus, electricity consumption to produce one kg of dry matter are 2857 (= 20.0/0.007) MJ/kg or 794 (= 2857/3.6) kWh.

more.unit: kWh/kg/year as printed (table cell, attributed to Graamans et al. 2017)
more.what: Indoor vertical farm lettuce energy use in the review table of Avgoustaki & Xydis 2020; much higher than other sources, probably a dry-matter basis; greenhouse row gives 60-180. Treat with caution.
more.quote: Energy use | 250 kWh/kg/year | Graamans et al. (2017)

biosphere2_area_per_person.unit: m2 of intensive cropping area per person (2000 m2 for 8 crew)
biosphere2_area_per_person.what: Biosphere 2 first closure 1991-1993, sunlit soil-based agriculture under glass, mostly vegetarian diet averaging 2200 kcal/person/day. It did not fully suffice: about 80% of nutritional needs were produced (Wikipedia says 83% of total diet), crew lost 10-20% body weight and reported continual hunger; farming and food processing took ~45% of crew time. The value 250 is 2000/8 (my division). Silverstone & Nelson 1996, Adv. Space Res. 18(4-5):49 (abstract). Wikipedia gives the agricultural biome as 2500 m2.
biosphere2_area_per_person.quote: The 2000 m2 cropping area provided about 80 percent of overall nutritional needs during the two years. Adaptation of the crew to the diet which averaged 2200 calories, 73 g. of protein and 32 g. of fat per person over the course of the two years. ... The crew experienced 10-20 percent weight loss, most of which occurred in the first six months of the closure

more.unit: percent of total diet produced
more.what: Wikipedia 'Biosphere 2' (raw wikitext).
more.quote: The agricultural system produced 83% of the total diet, which included crops of bananas, papayas, sweet potatoes, beets, peanuts, lablab and cowpea beans, rice, and wheat. Especially during the first year, the eight inhabitants reported continual hunger.

sunlight_dli_earth.unit: mol m-2 day-1 (monthly-averaged outdoor DLI at 30 deg latitude, winter to summer)
sunlight_dli_earth.what: Outdoor daily light integral: monthly averages 20-40 in the tropics, 15-60 at 30 deg latitude, 1-40 at 60 deg latitude; >70 on bright summer days at some locations (Wikipedia 'Daily light integral', citing Poorter et al. 2019). So mid-latitude summer is roughly 40-60.
sunlight_dli_earth.quote: Occasionally, values over 70 mol·m−2·d−1 can be reached at bright summer days at some locations. Monthly-averaged DLI values range between 20-40 in the tropics, 15-60 at 30° latitude and 1-40 at 60° latitude.

more.unit: mol m-2 day-1 (implied summer sunlight)
more.what: Bugbee & Salisbury 1989 call 150 mol m-2 d-1 '2.5 times summer sunlight', i.e. summer sunlight ~60 (my division).
more.quote: An integrated PPF of 150 mol m-2 d-1 (2.5 times summer sunlight) has produced 60 g m-2 d-1 of grain.

more.unit: umol per joule of PAR (400-700 nm) for a 5800 K (daylight) black-body spectrum
more.what: Conversion from PAR watts to PAR photons; multiply by the PAR fraction to convert total sunlight W/m2 to PPFD (about 1.9-2.0 umol/s per W of total surface sunlight using 42-43% PAR: my multiplication). Wikipedia 'Photosynthetically active radiation' table.

more.unit: fraction of surface sunlight energy in 400-700 nm (PAR fraction)
more.what: Sunlight at Earth's surface by energy: 52-55% infrared, 42-43% visible (400-700 nm), 3-5% UV (Wikipedia 'Sunlight', calculated from NREL reference spectra). For a 5800 K black body the fraction is 0.368 (PAR article); Wikipedia 'Photosynthetic efficiency' uses 53% in-band.
more.quote: In terms of energy, sunlight at Earth's surface is around 52 to 55 percent infrared (above 700 nm), 42 to 43 percent visible (400 to 700 nm), and 3 to 5 percent ultraviolet (below 400 nm).

more.unit: mol m-2 d-1 per (umol m-2 s-1 x hour of light)
more.what: DLI = 0.0036 x PPFD x light-hours; 1 umol m-2 s-1 for 24 h = 0.0864 mol m-2 d-1.
more.quote: Thus, 1 μmol m−2 s−1 = 0.0864 mol m−2 d−1 if light intensity stays the same for the entire 24 hour period.

radiation_use_efficiency_c3.unit: g dry biomass per MJ of intercepted TOTAL solar radiation
radiation_use_efficiency_c3.what: Wheat (C3) ~1.2 g/MJ and soybean ~1 g/MJ on a total solar basis (total solar is about double PAR), after Sinclair & Muchow 1999, as stated in Wu et al. 2016, Front. Plant Sci. 7:1518.
radiation_use_efficiency_c3.quote: In contrast, for C3 species, the RUE of wheat is ~1.2 g/MJ, whereas soybean, which is a dicotyledonous legume crop with a different leaf structure, has a RUE of ~1 g/MJ (Sinclair and Muchow, 1999).

more.unit: g dry biomass per MJ of PAR (and 1.4 g per MJ of total solar)
more.what: Typical wheat RUE. Moroyoqui-Parra et al. 2024, Crop Science, doi 10.1002/csc2.21115.
more.quote: In wheat crops, RUE is typically in the region of 2.8 g MJ−1 of photosynthetically active radiation (PAR, 400–700 nm) (Molero et al., 2019; Yunusa et al., 1993) and 1.4 g MJ−1 of solar radiation (Sinclair & Muchow, 1999).

more.unit: g total dry biomass per mol of PAR photons
more.what: C3 crops (wheat, soybean, lettuce, potato, tomato) in NASA Biomass Production Chamber; edible biomass 0.2-0.6 g/mol; corn (C4) under optimal field conditions listed as 0.7 g/mol. Wheeler et al. 2003.
more.quote: These radiation conversion efficiencies for the C3 crops in the BPC ranged from ~0.4 to 0.9 g mol-1 for total biomass and ~0.2 to 0.6 g mol-1 for edible biomass (Table 7). These results compare favorably with the 0.7 g mol-1 conversion value listed for corn (C4) canopies under optimal field conditions (Norman and Arkebauer, 1991).

more.unit: MJ dry matter per MJ absorbed PAR (conversion efficiency, dimensionless)
more.what: Mean conversion efficiency of C3 non-legume crops from 164 studies; C3 legumes 0.028-0.035; C4 food crops 0.046-0.049; biofuel crops 0.049-0.066. Slattery & Ort 2015, Plant Physiol. (abstract).
more.quote: ε(c) was greatest in biofuel crops (0.049-0.066), followed by C4 food crops (0.046-0.049), C3 nonlegumes (0.036-0.041), and finally C3 legumes (0.028-0.035).

radiation_use_efficiency_c4.unit: g dry biomass per MJ of intercepted TOTAL solar radiation
radiation_use_efficiency_c4.what: Maize (C4) under optimal growing conditions, up to 1.9; pearl millet ~2.0; sorghum 1.2-1.4. Total-solar basis (about double PAR). Wu et al. 2016, Front. Plant Sci. 7:1518.
radiation_use_efficiency_c4.quote: Based on a total solar radiation basis (which is approximately double the photosynthetic active radiation), the RUE of maize under optimal growing conditions is 1.6–1.7 g/MJ, but can be as high as 1.9 g/MJ (Lindquist et al., 2005).

more.unit: g dry biomass per MJ of intercepted PAR
more.what: Maize across diverse world locations, negatively correlated with vapour pressure deficit (Stockle & Kiniry 1990), quoted in Stockle & Kemanian 2020, Front. Plant Sci. 11:737.
more.quote: Stöckle and Kiniry (1990) summarized e data for maize across diverse world locations, and found that e fluctuating from 2.9 to 4.4 g/MJ PAR was negatively correlated to D.

light_saturation_c3.unit: umol m-2 s-1 PPF (leaf light saturation)
light_saturation_c3.what: Potato (C3) leaves at ambient CO2 in the field (Chapman & Loomis 1953: 3000 foot-candles); rises to ~820 at 2x CO2 and ~1015 at 5x CO2. Quoted in Wheeler, Fitzpatrick & Tibbitts 2019, Front. Plant Sci. 10:1632.
light_saturation_c3.quote: Chapman and Loomis (1953) reported increased photosynthetic rates for potato leaves under elevated [CO2] in field settings, and showed that light saturation could be increased by [CO2] enrichment from 3,000 foot-candles [approximately 585 µmol m−2 s−1 photosynthetic photon flux (PPF)], to 4,200 foot-candles (approximately 820 µmol m−2 s−1 PPF) at 2X ambient [CO2], and to 5,200 foot-candles (approximately 1,015 µmol m−2 s−1 PPF) at 5X ambient [CO2]

more.unit: percent of full sunlight
more.what: General statement for C3 leaves (soybean breeding review, Singh-Bakala et al. 2026, Theor. Appl. Genet., citing Zhu et al. 2012). With full sun ~2000 umol m-2 s-1 this is ~500 (my multiplication; the 2000 figure is not from this source).
more.quote: Because C3 leaf photosynthesis typically saturates at approximately 25% of full sunlight, upper canopy light saturation and lower canopy light limitation represent a primary structural bottleneck to radiation use efficiency (RUE) (Zhu et al. 2012).

more.unit: mol m-2 d-1 (DLI beyond which most plant traits approach saturation)
more.what: Whole-plant dose-response (Wikipedia 'Daily light integral', citing Poorter et al. 2019): growth strongly limited below 5.
more.quote: Generalised dose-response curves show that DLI is particularly limiting individual plant growth and functioning below 5 mol·m−2·d−1, whereas most traits approach saturation beyond a DLI of 20 mol·m−2·d−1.

light_saturation_c4.what: No numeric PPFD found. Qualitative only: maize (C4) leaves were reported not saturated at near full sunlight (Hesketh & Musgrave 1962), whereas early work held all plants saturate below 50% of sunlight. Wikipedia 'C4 carbon fixation' (raw wikitext). Crop-level: wheat canopies (C3) at high density also respond almost linearly up to 2000 umol m-2 s-1 (see cea_light_ppfd).
light_saturation_c4.quote: Later in 1958–1963 at Cornell University, field grown maize was reported to have much greater leaf photosynthetic rates of 40 μmol CO2·m−2·s−1 and not be saturated at near full sunlight.

wheat.what: cardinal temperatures for thermal-time (development) in APSIM-Wheat
wheat.quote: three cardinal temperatures of wheat, i.e. 0 °C (base), 26 °C (optimum), and 34 °C (maximum) as in APSIM-Wheat (Eqs (1) and (2)) (Zheng et al., 2014)
wheat.also: FAO: minimum daily temperature for measurable growth about 5 C; optimum mean daily temperature 15-20 C for growth and tillering (see growing_season_temperature)

maize.what: cardinal temperatures used for the temperature effect on radiation use efficiency of maize (base lower 8, optimum plateau 30-37, base upper 45)
maize.quote: using the cardinal temperatures 8°C (Tb1, base lower), 30°C (To1, base optimum), 37°C (To2, upper optimum), and 45°C (Tb2, base upper)
maize.also: Wikipedia 'Growing degree-day': corn starts growing at 10 C and stops at 30 C for modified GDD

rice.what: bilinear phenology (development) model in ORYZA2000 as used by van Oort & Zwart 2018 (Glob. Change Biol.), values based on Van Oort et al. 2011 and Sanchez et al. 2014; no maximum given (no delay above 31 C assumed)
rice.quote: In this paper we simulated with a bilinear temperature response phenology model with a base temperature of 14°C, an optimum temperature of 31°C and no delay in development at temperatures above 31°C, with values of 14°C and 31°C based on (Van Oort et al., 2011) and (Sanchez, Rasmussen, & Porter, 2014).

potato.what: FAO crop information: optimum mean daily temperature 18-20 C; tuber growth sharply inhibited below 10 C and above 30 C; night temperature below 15 C needed for tuber initiation; optimum soil temperature 15-18 C (not formal cardinal temperatures)
potato.quote: Yields are affected by temperature and optimum mean daily temperatures are 18 to 20°C. In general a night temperature of below 15°C is required for tuber initiation. Optimum soil temperature for normal tuber growth is 15 to 18°C. Tuber growth is sharply inhibited when below 10°C and above 30°C.

soybean.what: FAO crop information: minimum for growth about 10 C (about 15 C for crop production); growth rates decrease above 35 C and below 18 C. Separately, cardinal temperatures for soybean GERMINATION are ca. 2 / 30 / 40 C (min/opt/max; PMC7000526)
soybean.quote: Soybean is relatively resistant to low and very high temperatures but growth rates decrease above 35°C and below 18°C. In some varieties, flowering may be delaXed at temperatures below 24°C. Minimum temp-eratures for growth are about 10°C and for crop production about 15°C.
soybean.also_quote: Mean cardinal temperatures (minimum, optimum, and maximum) for germination were ca. 2, 30, and 40°C, respectively with significant differences among cultivars.

cardinal_temperatures.what: Base, optimum and maximum temperatures per crop; each crop carries its own source and quote. Note these are model/extension values for different processes (development, RUE, tuber growth), not one harmonised dataset; the Porter & Gawith 1999 and Sanchez et al. 2014 review tables themselves could not be opened (paywalled).

maize.note: grain needs mean daily >15 C and frost-free; at 10-15 C grown mostly as forage; >20 C early varieties mature in 80-110 days, medium 110-140

wheat.note: spring wheat 100-130 days, winter wheat 180-250 days; GDD figure is for hard red wheat as printed in the Wikipedia table headed 'baseline 10 C'

potato.note: early varieties 90-120 days, medium 120-150, late 150-180; no GDD-to-maturity total found

growing_season_temperature.unit: degrees C (mean daily) and growing degree days (base 10 C)
growing_season_temperature.what: Temperature and heat-sum requirements. Temperatures from FAO Land & Water crop information pages (archived 2022-12-10); GDD from Wikipedia 'Growing degree-day' table (common GDD base temperatures there: 4.5 C wheat/barley, 8 C potato, 10 C maize).
growing_season_temperature.quote: The crop is grown in climates ranging from temperate to tropic during the period when mean daily temperatures are above 15°C and frost-free. ... With mean daily temperature of 10 to 15°C maize is mostly grown as a forage crop because of the problem of seed set and grain maturity under cool conditions.

more.unit: degrees C
more.what: Wheat: minimum daily temperature for measurable growth ~5 C; optimum mean daily 15-20 C; ripening 18 C or more. FAO crop information, wheat.
more.quote: For winter and spring wheat minimum daily temperature for measurable growth is about 5°C. Mean daily temperature for optimum growth and tillering is between 15 and 20°C. ... A dry, warm ripening period of 18°C or more is preferred.

more.unit: days
more.what: Wheat growing period. FAO crop information, wheat.
more.quote: The length of the total growing period of spring wheat ranges from 100 to 130 days while winter wheat needs about 180 to 250 days to mature.

more.unit: growing degree days, base 10 C, to crop maturity
more.what: Maize. Wikipedia 'Growing degree-day' table.
more.quote: |[[Maize|Corn (maize)]] |''Zea mays'' |800 to 2700 GDD to crop maturity

more.unit: growing degree days (table headed baseline 10 C), to maturity
more.what: Barley. Wikipedia 'Growing degree-day' table.
more.quote: |[[Barley]] |''Hordeum vulgare'' |125–162 GDD to emergence and 1290–1540 GDD to maturity

more.unit: growing degree days (table headed baseline 10 C), to maturity
more.what: Wheat (hard red). Wikipedia 'Growing degree-day' table.
more.quote: |[[Wheat]] (hard red) |''Triticum aestivum'' |143–178 GDD to emergence and 1550–1680 GDD to maturity

more.unit: days
more.what: Potato growing period by variety group. FAO crop information, potato.
more.quote: Potato varieties can be grouped into early (90 to 120 days), medium (120 to 150 days) and late varieties (150 to 180 days).

heat_yield_loss.unit: percent global yield loss per degree C increase in global mean temperature
heat_yield_loss.what: Average of four independent methods (grid models, point models, statistical regressions, field warming), without CO2 fertilization, adaptation or genetic improvement. This is per degree of global mean warming from the present climate, not strictly 'above the crop optimum'. Zhao et al. 2017, PNAS 114:9326 (abstract).
heat_yield_loss.quote: Without CO2 fertilization, effective adaptation, and genetic improvement, each degree-Celsius increase in global mean temperature would, on average, reduce global yields of wheat by 6.0%, rice by 3.2%, maize by 7.4%, and soybean by 3.1%.

photosynthesis_red_dwarf.unit: (qualitative; Fv/Fm K dwarf 0.781 vs solar 0.777 for garden cress)
photosynthesis_red_dwarf.what: K dwarf (first experiment): garden cress (Lepidium sativum) under a simulated 4300 K (K4.5) star spectrum grew and photosynthesised comparably to solar illumination (dry mass slightly but not significantly lower; Fv/Fm 0.781 +/- 0.017 K dwarf vs 0.777 +/- 0.006 solar on day 9) despite ~3x lower PPFD; the cyanobacterium Chroococcidiopsis did significantly better under K-dwarf light. Vilovic, Schulze-Makuch & Heller 2024, arXiv:2405.19180.
photosynthesis_red_dwarf.quote: We find that garden cress Lepidium sativum under K-dwarf radiation exhibits comparable growth and photosynthetic efficiency as under solar illumination on Earth. The cyanobacterium Chroococcidiopsis sp. CCMEE 029 exhibits significantly higher photosynthetic efficiency and culture growth under K dwarf radiation compared to solar conditions.

more.unit: (qualitative)
more.what: M dwarf (M7 simulated spectrum, same PAR of 20.3 umol m-2 s-1 as the solar control; M7 total 57.6 umol in 380-780 nm): microalgae grew and photosynthesised similarly under M7 and solar light; the moss Physcomitrium patens grew less; Arabidopsis thaliana grew but with a shade-avoidance response and lower biomass than under solar (solar > M7 > far-red), with no difference in Fv/Fm. Battistuzzi et al. 2023, Life 13:1641.
more.quote: SOL-acclimated seedlings showed the highest biomass, followed by M7-acclimated seedlings and, finally, FR-acclimated seedlings. Fluorescence measurements after 9 days (Table 3) again showed no differences between the photosynthetic efficiency of SOL and M7-acclimated samples.

more.unit: umol photons m-2 s-1 PAR at the surface of Proxima Centauri b (about 3% of Earth's)
more.what: PAR available on an M-dwarf habitable-zone planet, quoted in Battistuzzi et al. 2023.
more.quote: Proxima Centauri b experiences on its surface irradiance of about 64–132 µmol photons m−2 s−1 (PAR) or about 3% that of the Earth [16].

more.unit: fraction of simulated M7 photons (380-780 nm) that fall in PAR 400-700 nm (20.3 of 57.6 umol; my division)
more.what: Spectral make-up of the simulated M7 starlight vs solar simulator (20.3 of 27.4 = 0.74). Battistuzzi et al. 2023.
more.quote: SOL light had about 27.4 µmols of photons m−2 s−1 (5.6 W m−2) in the whole working range (380–780 nm), of which 20.3 µmols of photons m−2 s−1 (4.4 W m−2) in the PAR (400–700 nm); M7 had about 57.6 µmols of photons m−2 s−1 (10.2 W m−2) in the whole working range, of which 20.3 µmols of photons m−2 s−1 (4.3 W m−2) in the PAR

par_fraction_k_star.unit: fraction of total emitted radiation in 400-700 nm, for a 4000 K BLACK BODY
par_fraction_k_star.what: Not a measured K-star value: black-body PAR fraction from the Wikipedia PAR table, 0.0809 at 3000 K, 0.208 at 4000 K, 0.368 at 5800 K. K dwarfs span roughly 3900-5300 K, so a black-body K star lies between 0.208 and 0.368 (the bracket is my reading; real K-star spectra with line blanketing differ). No source giving the fraction for an actual K-type stellar spectrum was found.

not_found: cea_yield_strawberry (no per-m2 yield under artificial light or high-tech greenhouse found in an openable source)
light_saturation_c4: numeric PPFD (only the qualitative 'not saturated at near full sunlight' for maize)
par_fraction_k_star for a real K-star spectrum (only black-body 4000 K and 5800 K values recorded)
cea_lighting_power: a directly stated W/m2 for a commercial vertical farm (recorded metered kWh/m2/day for an LED trial, NASA BPC 2 kW/m2 HPS, and greenhouse HPS 160-280 W/m2 instead)
sunlight W/m2-to-PPFD factor for TOTAL sunlight as a single stated number (recorded 4.56 umol/J of PAR and PAR fraction 0.42-0.43 separately)

cardinal_temperatures: the Porter & Gawith 1999 (wheat) and Sanchez et al. 2014 (maize, rice) review tables (paywalled; crop-model values recorded instead); rice maximum; formal potato and soybean growth cardinals
growing_season_temperature: GDD to maturity for potato; minimum growing-season temperature for barley

NASA BIO-Plex-specific area-per-person figure; Wheeler 2008 'Crop productivities and radiation use efficiencies' (Adv. Space Res. 41:706) abstract; Wheeler 2017 'Agriculture for space' (publisher page refused automated access)

_notes.retrieval: Web search was unavailable in this session (budget exhausted); all figures were read from pages fetched directly: Europe PMC REST API (open-access full text or abstract), NASA NTRS PDFs, arXiv PDF, Wikipedia raw wikitext, Internet Archive copies of FAO pages. Sources marked '(abstract)' were read as the abstract only.
_notes.shape: Each slug has the requested keys; where one slug needed several figures, extra entries of the same shape are under 'more'. cardinal_temperatures and growing_season_temperature carry a per-crop object in 'value'.
_notes.quotes: Quotes are copied from the fetched text; wiki markup/table separators kept or lightly trimmed ('...' marks omitted text; OCR errors in the NASA 2003 PDF text were normalised, e.g. '-0.4' read as '~0.4'). NASA Table 7 rows were read from a scanned, rotated table image, so they are transcriptions of table rows, not extracted text.
